opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think people often conflate the two, and it's worth pulling them apart.

The architecture question is basically: can the model physically *hold* and *access* that much information? At hundreds of millions of tokens, vanilla attention just doesn't work. The quadratic cost becomes absurd, and even with linear-ish variants you hit memory bandwidth limits. So you end up looking at things like state-space models, recurrence, retrieval-augmented setups, or some kind of compressive memory. Those are all architectural bets about *how* information flows through the system.

The learning paradigm question is different. Even if your architecture can technically ingest 100 million tokens, does the model actually *learn* to use them? This is where I think a lot of the long-context work has been a bit misleading. You can pass a needle-in-a-haystack test without really reasoning over the whole context. Retrieving one fact is very different from synthesizing information spread across a huge corpus. Getting a model to do the latter depends on the training objective, the data mixture, and whether there's any signal during pretraining or post-training that rewards long-range dependencies. And honestly, naturally occurring data with real dependencies at that scale is pretty rare.

So my mental model is that architecture sets the ceiling, and the learning paradigm decides how close you get to it. You can have a beautiful architecture that's effectively wasted because the model never learned to exploit the context. Or you can have a clunky architecture where the training is so well designed that it does surprisingly well.

There's also a deeper question about whether at that scale you even want everything "in context," versus something closer to continual learning, where you push information into the weights. That blurs the line, because now the learning paradigm *is* the memory mechanism. My intuition is that the most interesting progress will come from people who treat these as one co-design problem instead of optimizing each separately. That's very much an open research area, though, and I wouldn't claim anyone has it figured out.

r001.rationale: The response assigns a physical context limit to architecture and discusses learning as whether the model uses the context; it does not locate the limitation in gradient descent or backpropagation.

r002.rationale: It describes architecture as shaping information flow, but does not characterize it as the interface between the learning algorithm and the tokens.

r003.rationale: It raises continual learning as an alternative at this scale, describing information being pushed into the weights instead of keeping everything in context.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think people conflate these two a lot, and it's worth pulling them apart. When I say architecture, I mean the inductive bias of the model itself — is it a transformer, is it a state space model, is it some hybrid, what does the attention pattern look like, how does information flow through the layers. The learning paradigm is a different axis entirely. That's about how you train the thing — is it next-token prediction, is it some kind of denoising objective, is it RL, how do you curriculum the context length, what does the data look like.

And I think the mistake people make with long context specifically is they treat it as purely an architecture problem. Like, "oh, attention is quadratic, so we need linear attention, so we need SSMs, problem solved." And that's not wrong exactly, but it's really only addressing the compute side. It says nothing about whether the model actually learns to use a hundred million tokens of context.

Because honestly, the architecture can in principle attend to everything, and the model can still be terrible at retrieving or reasoning over stuff that's a long way back. That's not an architecture failure, that's a learning failure. The model never saw enough training signal where attending that far back was actually rewarded. Most natural text just doesn't have dependencies that span millions of tokens, so if you just scale context and train on web data, you get a model that technically has a long window but behaves like it has a short one.

So the way I think about it is: architecture sets the ceiling on what's representable and what's tractable. The learning paradigm determines how much of that ceiling you actually reach. And at hundreds of millions of tokens, I'd argue the learning side is the harder and more underexplored problem. You can make the architecture scale with a lot of engineering — people have done this. Making the model actually care about token ten million when it's generating token a hundred million, that's a data and objective question, and we don't have great answers yet.

The other thing I'd add is they're not fully independent. Certain architectures make certain learning paradigms easier. If you have a fixed-size recurrent state, you're asking the model to compress everything, and that pushes you toward objectives that teach it what's worth keeping. If you have full attention, you can be lazier about compression but you need to teach it to search. So the choices interact, but I still find it clarifying to ask separately: what can this model represent, and what have I actually trained it to do.

r001.rationale: The response says long-context use is mainly a learning problem, but it does not locate the limitation in gradient descent or backpropagation, and it also assigns architecture a role in representability and tractability.

r002.rationale: It describes architecture as the model’s inductive bias and information flow, but does not characterize it as the interface between the learning algorithm and the tokens.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose continual learning as an approach to contexts of hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.

astra-6.text:
I think those are two separate questions. Architecture is about how you process the tokens—what the computation looks like, how information moves through the model, and how expensive that is. The learning paradigm is about what you ask the model to learn from those tokens and how you train it to do that.

So when you say hundreds of millions of tokens, do you mean processing that many tokens over training, or giving the model that much information in a single context? Those are very different problems. An architecture might make a huge context computationally feasible, but that doesn’t automatically mean the model learns to use information across that context. You still need a training objective and data that reward that behavior.

For me, the interesting part is the interaction: the architecture gives you a capability, and the learning paradigm determines whether you actually learn to exploit it.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes architecture from learning and says training must teach the model to use long-context information, but it does not identify gradient descent or backpropagation as the limiting factor.

r002.rationale: It describes architecture as the computation and information flow over tokens, but does not characterize it as the interface between the learning algorithm and the tokens.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose continual learning as an approach to processing hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are two different axes. Architecture is about how you parameterize the computation—whether you use attention, recurrence, or some kind of memory, and what the computational cost looks like. The learning paradigm is about what you train the model to do and how it learns to use that computation.

So when you say hundreds of millions of tokens, the question is: are those tokens all in a single context, or is the model processing them over time and learning from them? Those are very different problems. An architecture might let you stream through that many tokens efficiently, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the model can retain and use the relevant information.

For me, the interesting question is what training signal teaches it to remember, what to forget, and how to retrieve something when it becomes useful later. Architecture gives you the mechanism, but the learning paradigm has to make that mechanism useful.

r002.rationale: It describes architecture as parameterizing computation and providing a mechanism, but does not characterize it as the interface between the learning algorithm and the tokens.
